deep.reconstruction:
The page contains no mathematics. It is a fair-copy page of lecture or school notes on ancient history, in German Kurrent script, in the section 'Verbreitung der Phönizier durch Kolonien' (Spread of the Phoenicians through colonies). It continues from the previous page (history of Sidon and Tyre) and leads into the next page (Phoenician sea trade, then 'V. Geschichte der Juden'). The hand and the content suggest a pupil's or student's notebook kept among the Gauss papers, possibly belonging to a family member, rather than Gauss's own research notes. The content, point by point:

(1, continued) General ideas on colonies. When a nation trades in distant lands whose inhabitants are still 'raw', depots (Niederlagen) must exist. In antiquity colonies were a means of necessity or utility (reading uncertain).

(2) Relation of the colonies to the mother city. The colonies were independent and could be, because the Phoenicians were not a conquering people. Still a close bond persisted. Each side felt it owed the other duties: not to injure one another, and to assist one another.

(3) Date of founding. It cannot be given exactly. Almost all colonies were founded in the most flourishing period, between 1000 and 600 (BCE implied).

(4) Survey of the colonies. They lay chiefly on the shores of the Mediterranean. Sicily, Spain and North Africa were the main colonial lands. The most important places were Gades and Carthage ('Gades das heutige Cadix').

(Handel der Phönicier) Trade. Their land trade went partly to Arabia, for frankincense, other aromatics, camel-hair yarn and fine wool. It went partly to Armenia, for slaves, metals, horses and mules (sentence completed on the next page).

There is no derivation, formula or computation to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical content, so there are no mathematical errors.

Historically, the date range 1000-600 (BCE) is a conventional textbook simplification. Ancient tradition dates Gades to c. 1100 BCE and Carthage to 814/813 BCE (the previous page gives c. 880). Within the conventions of early-19th-century school history this is acceptable.
